headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers - one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper - so it cannot describe either condition in general, only what these two specific papers report.

Both papers show real impairment to work/employment and quality of life, but they measure it with completely different tools (percentage-point gaps in disability and misdiagnosis for Lyme disease vs. standardized productivity and SF-36 scores for Long COVID), so the numbers cannot be directly compared.

Neither paper reports any dollar-denominated cost figures, and both flag that their burden estimates are not broken down by demographic subgroup, leaving a shared blind spot in both conditions' evidence base.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports a 22 percentage-point gap in self-reported inability to work between persistent Lyme disease patients and acute Lyme disease patients.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports a 7.5-point gap in absolute presenteeism score (WHO HPQ, 0-100 scale) between the long COVID group and the asymptomatic group at 36 months, plus a 28.7 percentage-point gap in self-reported worsened economic condition between continuous-symptom and recovered-symptom patients.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers show meaningful work-related burden, but readers should not treat a percentage-point disability gap and a standardized productivity-score gap as the same kind of number.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports a 38 percentage-point gap in fair/poor self-rated health between persistent Lyme disease patients and acute Lyme disease patients.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports a 4.1-point gap in SF-36 quality-of-life score (0-100 scale) between the long COVID group and the asymptomatic group at 36 months.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both conditions show a measurable quality-of-life penalty in these papers, even though the measurement scales differ and cannot be converted into one another.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports a 31 percentage-point gap in prior-misdiagnosis prevalence between persistent and acute Lyme disease patients, and separately that 74% of persistent Lyme disease patients reported any prior misdiagnosis.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report any diagnostic delay or misdiagnosis data.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Diagnostic delay is a documented driver of burden in the Lyme disease paper but is simply not addressed in the Long COVID paper, so no comparison is possible on this point.

comparison_rows.dimension: Out-of-pocket and direct medical cost evidence

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports no dollar-denominated medical costs, out-of-pocket costs, or lost-income figures anywhere in its analysis.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper also reports no dollar-denominated cost data; its economic measures are limited to standardized productivity and quality-of-life scores and a self-reported categorical 'economic condition' rating.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Readers looking for actual cost-of-illness figures will not find them in either paper, which limits any policy or payer use of this comparison for budgeting purposes.

comparison_rows.dimension: Access barriers (trial eligibility and insurance coverage)

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports that commonly used clinical trial eligibility criteria exclude about 90% of real-world persistent Lyme disease patients, and separately notes that about 50% of Lyme disease patients are treated by clinicians whose services are not covered by insurance.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not report any trial-eligibility or insurance-coverage access data.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Access-to-research and access-to-covered-care barriers are a central finding in the Lyme disease paper with no counterpart measured in the Long COVID paper.

comparison_rows.dimension: Systemic gaps / how burden may be undercounted by official data or research systems

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper describes a structural gap in which restrictive trial eligibility criteria produce small, non-generalizable trials and leave clinicians without adequate treatment guidance, a pattern the paper itself frames as a systemic research gap.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not describe a comparable systemic research-access gap; it instead notes methodological limits such as the lack of a healthy control group and possible misclassification of reinfection as long COVID.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two papers flag different kinds of structural weaknesses in the evidence base, so 'undercounting' means something different in each case and should not be treated as the same issue.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports its eligibility, misdiagnosis, disability, and health-status figures only as pooled persistent-vs-acute values, without breaking them down by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or other subgroups, even though the two subgroups differ in sex composition.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports its presenteeism, absenteeism, and quality-of-life figures only as pooled values by long COVID status, symptom trajectory, or symptom cluster, without breaking them down by sex, age, or other demographic subgroups despite collecting that data.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: In both papers, a reader cannot tell whether the burden falls more heavily on particular demographic groups, which limits targeted policy responses for either condition.

shared_themes.theme: Both the Lyme disease paper and the Long COVID paper document substantial impairment to patients' ability to work, even though they use entirely different measurement tools.

evidence.note: Reports a 22 percentage-point gap in self-reported inability to work between persistent and acute Lyme disease patients.
Reports a 7.5-point gap in work-productivity (presenteeism) score and a 28.7 percentage-point gap in self-reported worsened economic condition by symptom trajectory.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers show measurably worse quality of life for the more severely affected patient subgroup.

evidence.note: Reports a 38 percentage-point gap in fair/poor self-rated health between persistent and acute Lyme disease patients.
Reports a 4.1-point gap in SF-36 quality-of-life score between the long COVID group and the asymptomatic group at 36 months.

shared_themes.theme: Neither paper provides any dollar-denominated cost figures, so economic burden in both cases is described only through proxy measures (disability/health-status percentages for Lyme disease, standardized productivity and quality-of-life scores for Long COVID).

evidence.note: States explicitly that no medical cost, out-of-pocket cost, lost-income, or caregiving-time figures are reported anywhere in the document.
States explicitly that no dollar-denominated cost-of-illness estimate exists, and that converting its standardized scores to costs would require external wage or healthcare-price data.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers report their burden findings only in pooled form, without breaking results down by demographic subgroup, despite having some subgroup data available.

evidence.note: The subgroup disaggregation limitation notes that sample-yield and prevalence figures are pooled by persistent-vs-acute status only, despite Table 1 showing the two subgroups differ by sex.

The subgroup disaggregation limitation notes that productivity and quality-of-life scores are pooled by long COVID status, trajectory, or cluster, without breakdown by sex or age despite that data being collected.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper documents a specific research-access barrier: restrictive clinical trial eligibility criteria exclude the large majority of real-world persistent Lyme disease patients.

evidence.note: Finds that commonly used eligibility criteria would exclude about 90% of real-world persistent Lyme disease patients from clinical trials.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper identifies a large diagnostic-delay/misdiagnosis gap tied to disease duration, which the Long COVID paper does not address.

evidence.note: Reports a 31 percentage-point gap in prior-misdiagnosis prevalence between persistent and acute Lyme disease patients, with 74% of persistent patients reporting any prior misdiagnosis.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper notes that half of Lyme disease patients are treated by clinicians whose services are not covered by insurance, an access-to-covered-care barrier not addressed in the Long COVID paper.

evidence.note: States that about 50% of Lyme disease patients are treated by clinicians whose services are not covered by insurance, citing the authors' prior survey work.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper shows that burden varies by symptom trajectory over a 3-year follow-up, with continuous-symptom patients reporting worse work and economic outcomes than patients whose symptoms resolved.

evidence.note: Reports that 43.6% of continuous-symptom patients reported worsened economic condition at 36 months, compared with 14.9% of recovered-symptom patients.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither the Lyme disease paper nor the Long COVID paper reports any direct medical cost, out-of-pocket cost, or other dollar-denominated figure for either condition.
Neither paper quantifies caregiving time or family/household cost burden, even though both describe disability or reduced work capacity that plausibly creates caregiving need.
Neither paper breaks its burden findings down by demographic subgroup (sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, etc.), despite both having collected at least some such data.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers two papers - one on Lyme disease (persistent vs. acute, from a patient registry) and one on Long COVID (a 3-year hospitalized cohort in Japan) - so it describes only what these two specific papers report, not Lyme disease or Long COVID in general. Both papers show real, measurable burden in work capacity and quality of life for the more severely affected patients, but they use incompatible measurement tools (percentage-point health/disability gaps for Lyme disease vs. standardized productivity and SF-36 scores for Long COVID), so their numbers cannot be combined or directly compared. The Lyme disease paper additionally documents a research-access barrier (trial eligibility criteria excluding most real-world patients) and an insurance-coverage gap that the Long COVID paper does not address, while the Long COVID paper offers more granular tracking of how burden changes by symptom trajectory over time. Neither paper provides any dollar-denominated cost evidence, and both acknowledge that their findings are not broken down by demographic subgroup. This is not a controlled or representative comparison of the two conditions, only a juxtaposition of what these two independently produced papers happen to measure.
cross_analysis.limitations: This comparison is based on a very small, non-random sample: one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, with no papers covering both conditions together. Each paper was built from a single uploaded document using its own methods, population, and measurement instruments, so this is not a controlled study and no causal or magnitude comparisons across conditions should be drawn from it.

learning_cards.headline: Ask how often misdiagnosis happens before a Long COVID diagnosis
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found that patients with persistent Lyme disease report prior misdiagnosis 31 percentage points more often than patients with acute Lyme disease.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report any measure of misdiagnosis or diagnostic delay.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers track how often patients were misdiagnosed before receiving a Long COVID diagnosis?

learning_cards.headline: Ask about complete inability to work, not just reduced output
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found that patients with persistent Lyme disease report being unable to work 22 percentage points more often than patients with acute Lyme disease.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper measures reduced work performance while employed but does not report whether patients are completely unable to work.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers measure the share of patients who are entirely unable to work, not only reduced performance while working?

learning_cards.headline: Ask about performance loss among patients who still work
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper found the presenteeism score for patients without symptoms was 7.5 points higher than for patients with long COVID, on a 0-100 scale.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper reports whether patients can work at all but does not report a standardized score of work performance among those still working.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers use a standardized presenteeism tool to measure reduced work performance among persistent Lyme disease patients who remain employed?

learning_cards.headline: Ask for a standardized quality-of-life score, not just self-rating
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper found the SF-36 score for patients without symptoms was 4.1 points higher than for patients with long COVID, on a 0-100 scale.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper reports a percentage-point gap in fair/poor self-rated health but does not report a standardized multi-domain quality-of-life score like SF-36.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Lyme disease researchers administer a standardized quality-of-life instrument such as SF-36 to patients with persistent Lyme disease?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper could prompt the Long COVID paper to ask about misdiagnosis history and total work incapacity, while the Long COVID paper could prompt the Lyme disease paper to ask about standardized presenteeism and SF-36 scores, so the two measurement traditions could eventually be compared on common ground.
